# MarkdownView: Showing a Markdown Text as a Document

The file [`MarkdownView.tsx`](MarkdownView.tsx) is a **component**: a reusable piece of a
screen that an application puts into its window. It shows a **Markdown** text as a finished
document. Markdown is a simple text format: `# Title` is a heading, `- item` is a list,
`[text](other.md)` is a link. Files such as `README.md` are written in it.

The component only shows the text. It does not read files and does not open anything. The
application that uses it, the **host**, gives it the text and decides what a click on a link
means. Reco Studio uses it for its built-in Markdown viewer; any other application can use it
too.

What you will learn:

1. What the component gets from the host, and what it gives back
2. How a text becomes a document, and what happens with HTML inside the text
3. What a click on a link does, and how the host can allow more kinds of links
4. How headings get their names, so a link can jump to them
5. How images and code blocks work
6. Where the code is surprising

## The Problem

An application wants to show a Markdown text: a `README.md` in a preview, a note, a message.
The text can come from anywhere, also from a stranger. So the view must:

- show the usual parts of a document: headings, lists, tables, task lists, quotes, code,
  images and links
- never run a script that someone wrote into the text, and never jump to another page
- leave every decision about files and programs to the application, because only the
  application knows where the text came from

## Who Talks to Whom

![Diagram. On the left the host application (Reco Studio, Pilot or another one) reads the file and decides about links. It passes four things to MarkdownView: source (the Markdown text), linkSchemes (extra link schemes), resolveImage (image path to URL) and renderCode (own code blocks). Inside MarkdownView five steps follow each other: 1. react-markdown and remark-gfm turn the text into a tree of the document; 2. raw HTML is skipped (skipHtml); 3. link and image addresses are checked (urlTransform and linkSchemes); 4. headings get ids (rehypeHeadingIds); 5. images and code blocks (resolveImage, renderCode). The result is the page with headings, lists, tables, images and code. A green arrow goes back from the page to the host: a click on an #anchor link scrolls the view itself, any other link calls onLinkClick(href) of the host.][fig-who]

The component does not do the hard work of reading Markdown itself. It uses two libraries:
**react-markdown** turns the text into a document, and **remark-gfm** adds the parts that
GitHub knows (tables, task lists, strikethrough, links written as plain addresses). The
component adds its own rules around them: what to do with HTML, which addresses to keep, how
to name headings and what to do on a click.

## What It Can Do

The host sets the component with **props**, the settings of a component:

| Prop | What the host gives | What happens without it |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| `source` | The Markdown text (required) | — |
| `onLinkClick` | What to do when a link is clicked; it gets the address as written | A click on a link does nothing |
| `linkSchemes` | More kinds of addresses a link may keep, for example `['file']` | Only web and mail links are kept |
| `resolveImage` | How to turn an image path of the text into an address the window can load | The path is used as written |
| `renderCode` | Its own drawing of a code block, for example with colours | Code is shown as plain text in a box |
| `className` | A name for its own styles | — |

The file also gives out the function `slugify`, which makes the name of a heading (see
[Headings and Their Names](#headings-and-their-names)).

## From Text to Document

![On the left the source text of a sample document "Field Guide" with emphasis, inline code, strikethrough, three links, a heading Install, a task list with one done and one open item, a table of two rows, a quote, a bash code block with "make dist", an image img/chart.svg, a script line and a line with a bold tag. On the right a screenshot of the rendered view in dark colours: the heading Field Guide, the paragraph with bold README, italic emphasis, the code and the struck-through old text, blue links, the heading Install, two checkboxes (one ticked), the table, the quote with a grey bar, the code block, the chart image, and the last line "Inline raw HTML keeps only its text". The script line is not shown at all.][fig-render]

The picture is a real screenshot of the component with this text. Everything that Markdown
and GitHub know is drawn: headings, lists, task lists (the boxes cannot be clicked), tables,
quotes, code and images. The colours come from the theme of the application (VS Code theme
variables), with dark colours when the application has none.

**HTML inside the text** is skipped. Markdown allows HTML tags such as `<script>` or `<b>`;
a stranger could use them to run a program in the window. The component throws them away:

| HTML in the text | What the reader sees (real result) |
| ----- | ----- |
| A block `<script>alert(1)</script>` | Nothing |
| A block `<div style="color:red">red block</div>` | Nothing, also the text inside is gone |
| `<b>bold?</b> after` inside a line | `bold? after`: the tags are gone, the words stay |

## Where a Click on a Link Goes

![Table of ten links and what a click does, in two columns: without linkSchemes, and with linkSchemes set to file and javascript. #install scrolls to #install in both columns. other.md, ../guide/setup.md#part, https://example.com/a and mailto:team@example.com call onLinkClick of the host in both columns. file:///home/ann/notes.md does nothing without linkSchemes (href is empty) and calls the host with linkSchemes. javascript:alert(1), data:text/html,x, vscode://file/a and ftp://example.com/f do nothing in both columns. A note says that javascript: stays dropped even when the host lists it, and that the view never opens anything itself.][fig-links]

A click on a link never makes the window jump to another page. The component stops the
browser and decides itself:

- A link to a **heading of the same document** (`#install`) scrolls the view to the heading.
  The host is not asked. When no heading has that name, nothing happens
- **Every other kept link** goes to the host through `onLinkClick`, with the address exactly as
  written in the text (`../guide/setup.md#part`). The host decides: open a file, start the web
  browser, or nothing
- A link with a **removed address** does nothing

Which addresses are kept? By default only `http`, `https`, `irc`, `ircs`, `mailto` and `xmpp`,
plus addresses without a scheme (`other.md`, `#install`). A **scheme** is the first part of an
address before the colon: `https`, `file`, `javascript`. Any other scheme becomes an empty
address. With `linkSchemes` the host adds schemes for links, for example `file` in a desktop
application. Three schemes stay forbidden even when the host lists them: `javascript`,
`vbscript` and `data`, because they can run code or hide a page.

## Headings and Their Names

Every heading gets a **name** (an `id`), so a link `#name` can jump to it. The name is made the
same way as on GitHub, so links written for GitHub work here. These are real results:

| Heading | Name |
| ----- | ----- |
| `Open questions` | `open-questions` |
| `Open questions` (the second one) | `open-questions-1` |
| `Instalace a spuštění` | `instalace-a-spuštění` |
| `C++ & Go: 2 tips!` | `c--go-2-tips` |
| `snake_case-name` | `snake_case-name` |
| `␣␣Trim me␣␣` (spaces around) | `trim-me` |

The rule: remove the spaces at the start and the end, use small letters, drop every character
that is not a letter, a digit, a space, `_` or `-`, and turn each space into `-`. Letters of
every language stay, so a Czech heading keeps `š` and `ě`. A repeated name gets `-1`, `-2`, …

## Images and Code Blocks

An **image** path goes first through the address check, then to `resolveImage` of the host,
which makes an address the window can load. Real results with a host that turns a path into
`host-image://<path>`:

| Image in the text | Address in the page |
| ----- | ----- |
| `img/page.png` | `host-image://img%2Fpage.png` |
| `../shared/logo.png` | `host-image://..%2Fshared%2Flogo.png` |
| `https://example.com/x.png` | `host-image://https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fx.png` |
| `file:///home/ann/a.png` (also with `linkSchemes: ['file']`) | `host-image://` (empty path) |
| `data:image/png;base64,…` | `host-image://` (empty path) |

Images load only when they come near the visible part of the document (`loading="lazy"`), so a
long document with many images opens fast.

A **code block** is shown as plain text in a box. When the host gives `renderCode`, it gets the
code and its language (the word after the three backticks, for example `python`) and can draw
it with colours. When it answers "nothing" (`undefined`), the plain box is used.

## When Something Goes Wrong

| Situation | What the reader sees |
| ----- | ----- |
| The text has a script or other HTML | The HTML is not shown; the rest of the document is |
| A link has a forbidden scheme (`javascript:`) | The link text is shown; a click does nothing |
| A link jumps to a heading that does not exist | Nothing happens |
| An image cannot be loaded | The browser shows its usual empty image place |
| The host gives no `onLinkClick` | Only `#heading` links work |
| The text is empty | An empty view |

## Where the Code Is Surprising

### Inline images with `data:` never show

The address check runs before `resolveImage`, and it removes `data:` and every scheme that is
not on the list. `linkSchemes` does not help, because it is only for links. So the host gets an
**empty path** in `resolveImage` and must cope with it (Reco Studio keeps the empty path).

### A heading link with a broken `%` code throws an error

A link `#%E0` has a `%` code that is not a valid character. On a click, the component decodes
it with `decodeURIComponent`, which throws `URIError: URI malformed`. Nothing happens for the
reader, but the error appears in the console of the window. A link `#100%` is safe:
react-markdown writes it as `#100%25`.

### HTML in a line keeps its words

A whole HTML block disappears with its text, but HTML tags inside a line of text are removed
while the words between them stay. So `<b>bold?</b>` becomes plain `bold?`.

### Two spaces make two dashes

`C++ & Go: 2 tips!` becomes `c--go-2-tips`: `&` is dropped, the two spaces around it stay,
and each space becomes a dash. GitHub does the same, so the names match.

## For Developers: Where to Look in the Code

| Topic | Where |
| ----- | ----- |
| Settings of the component | `MarkdownViewProps` |
| Styles injected once into the page | the block at the top (`markdown-view-styles`) |
| Heading names | `slugify`, `rehypeHeadingIds`, `textOf` |
| Allowed addresses | `UNSAFE_SCHEMES`, `linkUrlTransform`, `urlTransform` in `MarkdownView` |
| HTML skipped | `skipHtml` on `<Markdown>` |
| Click on a link | `handleClick` |
| Images and code blocks | `components.img`, `components.pre`, `codeLanguage` |

## Words to Remember

| Word | Meaning |
| ----- | ----- |
| Component | A reusable piece of a screen that an application puts into its window |
| Host | The application that uses the component and gives it the text |
| Prop | A setting that the host gives to the component |
| Markdown | A simple text format for documents (`# Title`, `- item`, `[text](link)`) |
| GitHub-flavoured Markdown | Markdown with the extras of GitHub: tables, task lists, strikethrough |
| Raw HTML | HTML tags written inside a Markdown text |
| Scheme | The first part of an address before the colon: `https`, `mailto`, `file` |
| Anchor link | A link `#name` to a heading of the same document |
| Slug | The name of a heading made for links (`open-questions`) |
| Lazy loading | An image loads only when it comes near the visible part |
